extracted.intended_audience: regulated employers, stakeholder commenters, and regulatory/economic analysts reviewing the DOL overtime final rule
extracted.subtask_description: Economic-impact and cost-transfer methodology and assumptions used in the Department of Labor's final overtime rule (EAP exemptions), including time and wage assumptions, which costs are quantified vs. treated qualitatively, and sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory familiarization time estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 hour is an appropriate average estimate for the time each entity will spend reviewing the changes made by this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: EAP exemptions have existed since 1938 and recent rules in 2016 and 2019; employers who use the exemptions must apply them every time they hire an exempt-classified employee so they should be familiar. The Department will provide summaries and compliance assistance materials. The 1-hour estimate is an average across all entities, including those without affected or exempt workers (who likely spend little or no time). Sensitivity: using number of firms (6.4 million) rather than establishments (8.24 million) reduces Year 1 familiarization cost from $451.6M to $350.0M. The Department did not receive cross-industry data to overturn the 1-hour assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage rate and loading assumptions for familiarization and adjustment cost calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use compensation, benefits, and overhead rates applied to a standard SOC occupation to compute an all-in hourly rate (example: SOC 13-1141 median wage $32.59/hr; benefits 45% of base wage; overhead 17% of base wage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department used SOC 13-1141 (compensation, benefits and job analysis specialists) median wage $32.59/hr, applied 45% benefits and 17% overhead to derive $54.82/hr (2023 dollars). This all-in rate was used to value the 1-hour familiarization and the 75-minute adjustment time per affected worker. The Department relies on occupations and wage loadings consistent with previous WHD/DOL rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity count choice (establishments vs firms) and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary analysis uses number of establishments (8.24 million); sensitivity analysis using number of firms (6.4 million) reduces estimated total costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that using establishments yields higher aggregate cost estimates. It reports both the base calculation and the sensitivity alternative explicitly (e.g., Year 1 regulatory familiarization $451.6M using establishments; $350.0M using firms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment costs estimation components
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate adjustment costs, three pieces of information must be estimated: (1) a wage level for the employees making the adjustments; (2) the amount of time spent making the adjustments; and (3) the estimated number of newly affected EAP workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the methodological framework for calculating adjustment costs. The Department then applies its chosen wage (all-in $54.82/hr), time (75 minutes per affected worker), and estimated affected-worker counts to compute aggregate adjustment costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment time per affected worker
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department estimated that it will take establishments an average of 75 minutes per affected worker to make the necessary adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: same time estimate as used in the 2016 and 2019 rulemakings and the NPRM. Little applicable data were available to estimate time required. The Department uses per-worker rather than per-establishment estimates because the distribution of affected workers across establishments is unknown. Example conversions: establishment with 5 affected workers => 6.25 hours; 25 workers => 31.25 hours; 50 workers => 62.5 hours. The Department retains 75 minutes in the final rule absent representative opposing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of potential multiple adjustments due to phased threshold updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the compensation thresholds will undergo an initial update (July 1, 2024) and then an increase 6 months later using new methodologies, some employers may make two adjustments for affected workers; the Department includes potential additional adjustment costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To estimate multiple-adjustment costs, the Department identified workers earning at least $684/week but less than $844/week and estimated those likely to be raised to $844 at the initial update (Type 4 workers). It estimated 27,692 such workers and included associated extra adjustment costs, while noting uncertainty about how many employers would raise pay twice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-worker vs per-establishment time accounting decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustment costs and time estimates are applied per affected worker rather than per establishment because the distribution of affected workers across establishments is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains the reason for per-worker application and provides example per-establishment totals based on hypothetical numbers of affected workers per establishment. This choice affects aggregation and interpretation of firm-level burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial cost inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Managerial costs are applied only to workers who (1) become nonexempt, overtime-protected and (2) either regularly work overtime or occasionally work overtime, but on a predictable basis—an estimated 911,000 workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: most affected workers do not currently work overtime (69% Type 1) and thus would not require additional monitoring. Under these assumptions, management would spend an additional 10 minutes per week scheduling and monitoring each included affected worker. The Department computed additional managerial hours as ((10 minutes ÷ 60) × 911,000) = 151,800 hours per week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial time rate and calculation of managerial costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Managerial costs valued using median manager wage plus benefits and overhead: median hourly wage for a manager $51.62 (2022), 45% benefits, 17% overhead => $86.82/hr (2023 dollars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply weekly additional managerial hours (151,835) × 52 weeks × $86.82/hr to obtain estimated Year 1 managerial costs ($685.5 million). Managerial costs are expected to be incurred annually and vary with number of affected workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion/non-estimation of certain cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential reduction in cost to employers of determining employees' exemption status (duty-test relief for employees above the new salary threshold) is recognized but not quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the final rule firms will no longer be required to apply the duties test to the 8.7 million employees earning above the current standard salary ($684) and below the new standard salary ($1,128). The Department notes this is a cost savings to employers but did not estimate its size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of other potential costs (qualitative-only approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of potential costs (reduced scheduling flexibility; preference for salaried status; reduction in employer-provided benefits; increased prices; reduced services; reduced profits; hiring costs; hours-related worker effects; wage compression) are discussed qualitatively and generally not quantified due to lack of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each category the Department summarizes commenters' claims and cites relevant data or literature when available (e.g., CPS data on work-from-home; literature on wages and benefits), then explains why it did not quantify the cost (insufficient data, ambiguous net effects). Where possible, the Department explains channels and economic substitutions employers might use instead of quantifying dollar impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers estimation two-step approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfers (income redistribution from employers to employees) are estimated using a two-step approach: first identify affected EAP workers with an implicit regular hourly wage lower than the applicable minimum wage and calculate the wage increase necessary to reach the minimum wage; then estimate overtime payment transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overtime premium depends on the employee's regular rate of pay, so minimum-wage transfers and overtime transfers are linked. The Department reports separate estimates (e.g., Year 1 minimum wage transfers $87.5M; overtime transfers $1.4B) and aggregates total transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of implicit hourly wage and minimum-wage-transfer method
rubrics_metrics.description: Hourly rate of pay is calculated as usual weekly earnings divided by usual weekly hours worked; workers with implicit hourly rates below the applicable minimum wage are identified and their earnings adjusted upward to the minimum wage to compute transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: $684/week ÷ $7.25 = 94.3 hours needed to be below Federal minimum wage. The Department estimated only ~0.5% (19,900) of affected EAP workers earn an implicit hourly rate below the Federal minimum; it estimated mean increases in hourly wages, reductions in hours, and total annual transfer values (e.g., $87.5M Year 1). The Department also considers possible reduction in hours due to higher wages when calculating net effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor-demand elasticity assumptions for disemployment/hour-reduction effects
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate potential reductions in hours (disemployment effects) due to higher regular rates, the Department uses a labor demand elasticity of −0.2 for Year 1 and −0.4 for years 2–10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department chose these elasticities because they were used in the 2019 final rule and are consistent with other estimates used in the analysis. The elasticity is applied to percent changes in the regular rate of pay to estimate reductions in hours when computing transfers and related effects. The Department notes meta-analytic literature (Wolfson & Belman, etc.) and explains the choice relative to that literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of employer response alternatives in overtime-transfer estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may respond to workers becoming nonexempt by: (1) paying overtime premiums; (2) reducing overtime hours of affected workers and transferring hours; (3) reducing the regular rate of pay (subject to minimum wage constraints); (4) increasing affected workers' salaries to preserve exempt status; or (5) using a combination of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's estimates of overtime transfers depend on assumptions about how employers choose among these alternatives. The analysis discusses conceptual employer-response models (fixed-wage/labor demand vs fixed-job/employment contract) and uses worker earnings and hours distributions to predict responses and quantify transfers accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior-rule consistency as an evidentiary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where data are limited, the Department retains time and other parameter estimates used in its 2016 and 2019 rules (e.g., 1 hour familiarization; 75 minutes adjustment; 10 minutes/week managerial monitoring) absent representative contrary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly cites consistency with prior rules and the NPRM as supporting the chosen assumptions. It also notes when commenters provided survey responses or claims but lacked representative, cross-industry data to change assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical data citation and limits on quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department cites empirical sources (CPS, GSS, literature on minimum wage and price effects, meta-analyses) to support qualitative assessments but declines to quantify particular effects when data are insufficient or results are ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CPS data showing 74.2% of workers who worked at home were hourly; Lonnie Golden study on salaried worker flexibility; Peneva et al. (2015) on labor costs and price inflation. Where commenters made claims (e.g., employers will restrict flexible schedules), the Department sought evidence and did not quantify impacts when evidence was lacking.
